props.html:
Stain removal and surface restoration in Melbourne

When washing it has already failed

Some marks are not dirt. Rust, oil, tannin, efflorescence and overspray are in the material rather than on it, and more pressure makes them worse rather than better. Restoration is a chemistry problem with a dwell time, and sometimes it is a test patch and an honest answer.

  • Treatment matched to the stain
  • Test patch before committing the surface
  • We tell you when it will not come out
Get A Quote 0400 638 010
  1. Home
  2. Services
  3. Stain and surface restoration

On it, or in it

Everything on an outdoor surface is one of two things. It is on the surface, in which case cleaning removes it. Or it is in the surface, in which case cleaning only removes whatever is sitting on top of it and the mark is still there when the slab dries.

Concrete, aggregate, sandstone, bluestone and unsealed paving are all porous. They have open capillaries that draw liquid down and hold it. Engine oil, rust from a metal chair leg, tannin from leaf litter and the salts that come up through a new slab all end up below the wear surface. Getting them out means drawing them back up or breaking them down, with a product chosen for that specific stain, left on long enough to work, sometimes more than once.

Stain diagnosis

What it is, what shifts it, and what the result usually looks like

The last column is the one that matters. We would rather set the expectation now than at the end of a day on site.

Outcomes assume the stain has not been sealed over. A sealer applied on top of a stain locks it in, and the sealer has to come off first.
  What it actually is Treatment Realistic outcome
Rust Iron oxide drawn into the pores from furniture, reinforcing, fixings or bore water Oxalic or specialist rust remover, dwell, repeat Usually removed fully on concrete. Light aggregate can hold a faint shadow
Engine oil and grease Hydrocarbons absorbed below the wear surface Degreaser and a poultice that draws it back up, often twice Fresh spills come out well. Years-old oil usually leaves a halo
Leaf and bark tannin Plant acids from eucalypt and plane litter Alkaline treatment, then a neutral rinse Comes out almost completely, and returns if the litter is not managed
Efflorescence Salts migrating out of the concrete with moisture Acid wash at a controlled strength, then neutralised Removed, but it recurs until the moisture source is dealt with
Graffiti Aerosol paint, ink or etch on masonry, concrete or glass Solvent matched to the medium and the substrate, worked from the edge in Usually full removal. Porous brick can keep a ghost shadow
Paint and overspray Dried architectural or spray paint on hard surfaces Softening agent and mechanical lift, tested first Good on dense surfaces. Textured render rarely comes back perfect
Chewing gum Thermoplastic bonded to paving, usually commercial footpath Steam or freeze and lift, then the shadow treated Fully removed, including the dark shadow if it is caught early
Hard water and mineral Calcium and lime from sprinklers, bore water or render run off Mild acid, dwell, neutralise. On glass it depends on etching Good on stone and concrete. Etched glass is permanent
Tyre marks Plasticiser migrating out of the tyre into the slab Solvent and agitation, repeated Improves significantly. Deep marks in porous concrete often stay faint
Mortar and cement residue Builder splatter cured onto the surface Acid at controlled strength, checked against the substrate Removed. Acid etching is the risk, which is why strength is tested first

Swipe for the rest of the columns

Every unusual stain gets a test patch, and it is free

We pick a spot you will not look at, treat it, and let you see the result before the rest of the surface is committed. It costs you nothing and it is the only honest way to price a stain nobody has seen before. If the patch tells us the mark is permanent, we say so and you have not paid for a day of disappointment.

What makes a stain permanent

Three things, mostly. Time, because the longer a liquid sits the deeper it travels and the harder it is to draw back. Porosity, because an open surface like exposed aggregate or unsealed sandstone takes a stain much further down than dense trowelled concrete does. And what has been tried already, because the wrong product can set a stain or etch the surface around it, and sealing over a stain locks it in behind a layer that now has to come off first.

The fourth one, which is not really about the stain, is damage that looks like staining. Acid burn, efflorescence that has pitted the surface, and concrete that has lost its cream are surface failures rather than marks. Cleaning will not fix those, and anyone who tells you it will has not looked properly.

Which is why this family exists separately

Pressure cleaning and restoration are different trades using the same van. One is mechanical and fast, the other is chemical and slow. Most restoration jobs start as a cleaning job where one mark did not move, and the right answer is to stop pushing pressure at it.

Go straight to the stain

Eight restoration pages

Graffiti removalMasonry, concrete, glass and Colorbond, usually on a callout. Oil stain removalDriveways and garage floors, where the age of the spill decides the outcome. Rust stain removalFurniture legs, reinforcing, fixings and bore water on concrete and aggregate. Chewing gum removalCommercial footpaths and entries, steam or freeze and lift. Paint and overspray removalDried paint on hard surfaces, tested before anything is applied. Efflorescence removalThe white bloom on new concrete, brick and paving. Hard water and mineral stainsSprinkler, bore water and render run off on stone, concrete and glass. Mortar and cement residueBuilder splatter on brick, glass and hard surfaces after a build.

Questions

Asked about marks that will not wash off

Can you get an old oil stain out of my driveway?

Partly, almost always. Fully, it depends on how long it has been there and how porous the concrete is. A spill from last month usually comes out completely. A patch under where a car has been parked for ten years has travelled a long way down and generally ends up as a faint halo rather than invisible.

We will do a test patch so you can see which of those you are dealing with before paying for the work.

Will acid damage my concrete?

It can, which is why strength matters and why we test. Acid used too strong or left too long etches the surface and takes the cream off, leaving a patch that is lighter and rougher than everything around it. That is worse than the stain.

Used properly, at a controlled strength and neutralised afterwards, it is the right tool for efflorescence, mortar residue and mineral staining. The neutralising step is not optional and it is where cheap jobs cut corners.

Is graffiti removal urgent?

Yes, more than people expect. Fresh aerosol on a sealed or non-porous surface usually comes off cleanly. The same tag after a hot month has had the solvents drive the pigment into porous brick or block, and then you are looking at a shadow rather than a clean wall.

For commercial sites that get tagged repeatedly, an anti graffiti coating changes the economics: removal becomes a wash rather than a chemical job.

Can you remove stains from pavers without damaging the colour?

Usually. Coloured concrete pavers have their pigment through the body on good ones and only in the top layer on cheaper ones. A test patch tells us which you have in about ten minutes. Where the colour is only in a thin face, treatment is gentler and the realistic result is an improvement rather than a removal.

The previous cleaner made it worse. Can it be fixed?

Sometimes. The common ones we see are wand striping on concrete, acid burn around a treated spot, aggregate that has been stripped of stones, and a stain that has been sealed over. Striping and burn can often be evened out by treating the whole surface consistently. A sealed-in stain means stripping the sealer first, which is a bigger job but a real one.

Send photos. We will tell you honestly whether it is recoverable or whether you are better off resurfacing.

Do you restore surfaces as well as remove stains?

We clean and treat. We do not grind, resurface, repoint or repair concrete. Where a surface has failed rather than stained, that is a concreter's job and we will say so. What we can do afterwards is seal the result so it does not happen again.
